breaking: Science: two chemists share the 2026 Nobel Prize for explaining life's 'left and right hands'.
Peru: Machu Picchu tickets can no longer be reserved, only bought.

Sport: an influencer loses her sponsor after riding a bike in the Berlin Marathon.

articles.headline: Runner rides a bike in a marathon
articles.standfirst: A Chinese influencer said sorry after a photo showed her on a bicycle in the Berlin Marathon.
body: Sun Yuanyuan is a fitness influencer from China. More than 500,000 people follow her on the social media app Rednote. At the end of September she ran in the Berlin Marathon in Germany. A marathon is a race of 42 kilometres.

After the race, Sun said she had her best time ever. But then an Instagram page posted a photo. In the photo, Sun is sitting on the back of a bicycle. Another person is riding it. This happened between the 35th and the 40th kilometre of the race.
The page also showed her times for every 5 kilometres. She was much faster in that part of the race.

Sun wrote a message on Rednote. 'I felt ill during the race, but that is not an excuse,' she said. 'I broke the rules.' The race organisers took away her time. Her sponsor, the sports shoe company Brooks, also stopped working with her.

glossary.d: a person who has many followers on social media and can change what they buy or think
a company that gives money to a person or team, usually to advertise its products
a reason you give to explain why you did something wrong
a person who plans and runs an event
what you must and must not do in a game or a place

questions.q: How long is a marathon?
Who showed the photo of Sun on a bicycle?
Why was Sun faster between kilometres 35 and 40?
options: The road went down a hill.

questions.q: What did Sun say in her message?
options: Being ill was a good reason.

questions.q: What did Brooks do?

articles.headline: Machu Picchu: no more ticket problems?
articles.standfirst: Peru has changed the rules for buying tickets to visit the famous Inca city.
body: Machu Picchu is the most famous place to visit in Peru. Every year, thousands of tourists from all over the world go there. But for many weeks it was very difficult to get a ticket.
Why? Some people reserved many tickets but did not pay for them. Later, they sold the tickets again for more money. So other visitors could not find any tickets.

Now the Ministry of Culture has changed the rules. You cannot reserve a ticket any more. You must buy it immediately. On the website, you write your ID number and your name, and then you pay. You can also buy tickets in Machu Picchu Pueblo, the town near the Inca city.

The Culture Minister, Alberto Beingolea, says the problem is now over. At the start of October there were more than 1,000 tickets for October, 29,000 for November and more than 60,000 for December. The new rules are in a test period until 22 October.

glossary.d: to ask for something to be kept for you to use or buy later
a piece of paper or a code that shows you have paid to enter a place
a part of the government that is responsible for one area, like health or culture
now, without waiting
a time when people try something new to see if it works

questions.q: It was easy to get a Machu Picchu ticket in September.
Some people sold tickets again for more money.
Now you can reserve a ticket and pay later.
Tickets are cheaper for students.
There were more tickets for December than for November.

writing.task: You are going to visit Machu Picchu with your family. Write a message to your English friend (25 words or more). Say: when you are going, how you bought the tickets, and what you want to see there.

articles.headline: A swimming 'platypus' from the time of the dinosaurs
articles.standfirst: Scientists have described a fossil of a small furry animal that lived both in water and on land 165 million years ago.
body: About 165 million years ago, in the middle of the Jurassic period, huge dinosaurs were walking across the Earth. But in the rivers and lakes of what is now northern China, a much smaller animal was swimming and hunting. Scientists have now given it a name: Megacauda sungei.

Its fossil was found in 2015 in Inner Mongolia, but the full study has only just been published in the science journal Nature. The animal was not a true mammal but an early 'cousin' of mammals. It weighed between one and two kilograms – about the same as a modern platypus – which makes it the largest animal of its kind from that time.

Megacauda had webbed feet, a flat tail like an otter, very thick fur and a head similar to a dog's. These features suggest that it spent a lot of time in water. Unlike a platypus, however, it had strong, sharp teeth, so it probably ate small fish and salamanders. The rocks where it was found are full of salamander fossils.

Professor Zhe-Xi Luo of the University of Chicago, who led the study, said the fossil was 'stunningly complete', with almost all of its bones in place. According to the researchers, it shows that the ability to swim appeared very early in the history of mammals.

glossary.d: the remains of an animal or plant from a very long time ago, kept in rock
feet with skin between the toes, which help an animal to swim
a typical part or quality of something
a serious magazine where scientists publish their research
with all its parts; nothing is missing

questions.q: What is new about Megacauda sungei?
options: Scientists have now published a full study of it.
It is the first fossil found in Inner Mongolia.
It is the oldest dinosaur ever found.

questions.q: What does the writer say about the animal's size?
options: It was as big as a small dinosaur.
It was smaller than most animals of its kind.
It was similar in weight to a platypus today.
Scientists are not sure how heavy it was.

questions.q: Why do scientists think Megacauda spent time in water?
options: because of the shape of its feet and tail
because it was found in a lake
because it ate plants that grow in rivers

questions.q: How was Megacauda different from a platypus?
options: It had strong teeth for eating meat.

questions.q: What does the discovery show, according to the researchers?
options: Swimming developed early in mammal history.

articles.headline: Peru's satellite watches out for El Niño
articles.standfirst: The Peruvian Space Agency wants its satellite images to help the country prepare for heavy rain and floods.
body: Every few years, the water of the Pacific Ocean near Peru becomes warmer than usual. This is called El Niño, and it can bring very heavy rain, floods and landslides to the north of the country. Experts think another El Niño could arrive soon, so Peru is starting to prepare.

At the beginning of October, the Peruvian Space Agency, CONIDA, invited the organisations that deal with emergencies to a meeting at its satellite centre in Pucusana, south of Lima. Among the visitors were the heads of INDECI, the national civil defence institute, and CENEPRED, which studies disaster risks.

The aim of the meeting was to make sure that everyone can use the pictures taken by Peru's own satellite. With these images, the authorities can watch rivers and towns from space and find the areas that are most likely to flood. This information helps them decide where to act first and how to organise help more quickly.
'Space technology should be at the service of people,' is the message from CONIDA. If the authorities work together, they hope that the next El Niño will cause less damage than the ones in the past.

glossary.d: a large amount of earth and rock that falls down the side of a hill
a machine sent into space that goes around the Earth and sends back information or pictures
the people or organisations that have the power to make decisions for a country or area
the possibility that something bad will happen
to get ready for something that will happen

questions.q: Every few years the ocean near Peru becomes ___ than usual.
El Niño can ___ heavy rain and floods to the north of Peru.
CONIDA ___ the emergency organisations to a meeting.
The images help authorities find the areas most ___ to flood.
They hope the next El Niño will ___ less damage.

articles.headline: Golden Week: Chinese holidaymakers head south
articles.standfirst: A 13-day break at the start of October sent record numbers of Chinese travellers abroad – and Australia was one of their favourite destinations.
body: A. This year the calendar was kind to workers in China. The Mid-Autumn Festival fell right next to Golden Week, the national holiday that runs from 1 to 7 October, which gave many people a 13-day break. According to official immigration figures, more than 2.2 million passengers crossed China's borders during the festival, an increase of almost 17 per cent on last year.

B. One of the most popular destinations was Australia. Data from the International Air Transport Association showed that flight bookings from China to Australia for October were 19 per cent higher than twelve months earlier, and the booking platform Trip.com reported that travellers were choosing 'longer and further trips beyond the region'.

C. Fei Chang, who spent the holiday in Queensland's Whitsunday Islands with her husband, was surprised by how many fellow travellers she met. 'At some tourist spots, it felt like I could almost speak Mandarin to everyone,' she told the ABC.

D. The way people travel is also changing. Zhang Cheng, who runs a travel agency in Melbourne, says that many Chinese visitors are no longer interested in large coach tours that rush from one sight to the next. Instead, they prefer what she calls 'quality trips': small groups, or a road trip in a hired car where they can choose their own route.

E. Even so, the industry has not completely recovered. The number of Chinese visitors to Australia is still below the levels seen before the COVID-19 pandemic, and travel agents admit that it is hard to know exactly how many of their new customers come from China and how many are Chinese-speaking people who already live abroad.

glossary.d: the place where someone is going
an arrangement to have a seat, room or ticket at a particular time
someone who is in the same situation as you
to return to a normal or healthy state after a difficult period
to move or do something very quickly

articles.instructions: For each question, choose the paragraph (A–E). Each paragraph can be chosen once.

questions.q: Which paragraph mentions a personal experience of a tourist?
Which paragraph explains why the holiday was unusually long?
Which paragraph says that tourism has not yet returned to its earlier level?
Which paragraph describes a change in the style of travelling?

articles.headline: Citizens take Indonesia's government to court over choking haze
articles.standfirst: As forest fires burn for a fourth month, a group in West Kalimantan says the disaster could have been prevented.
body: For three months, a thick grey haze has hung over large parts of South-East Asia. It comes from fires burning in the peatlands of Indonesia – wet, carbon-rich ground that, once dry, can smoulder for weeks. The smoke has drifted across borders, forcing millions of people in Indonesia, Malaysia and Singapore to wear masks, and at times even hiding Singapore's best-known landmarks from view.

Now some of those affected have decided to fight back in court. This week a group of civil society organisations in West Kalimantan, on the island of Borneo, began a class action against the national government in the regional capital, Pontianak. The plaintiffs, who include Indigenous communities and youth groups, argue that the fires happen almost every year and that the authorities should have seen this season coming. 'El Niño had been predicted well before this dry season began,' said Glorio Sanen, the legal coordinator of the group Nafas Kalbar. 'Yet it seems we were not prepared.'

The group is asking the government to declare a national emergency, invest more in fire prevention, offer free health care to vulnerable people and prosecute those responsible for starting the fires. Their list of defendants is long: it includes the president, the vice-president, several ministers and the national police chief.

The health consequences are already serious. Indonesia's Health Ministry has recorded at least 175,000 cases of respiratory infection linked to the fires since August, and more than 200 fire spots were still burning this week. Relief is not expected soon: in most of the country, the rainy season will not arrive until November. The government, for its part, says it respects citizens' right to go to court and will respond through the legal process.

glossary.d: air that is difficult to see through because it contains smoke or dust
wet land made of old, partly decayed plants, which burns easily when it dries
a court case brought by a group of people who have all been affected in the same way
a person or group who starts a case against someone in court
easily hurt or affected, e.g. children, old or sick people

options: why peat fires are especially difficult to stop.

questions.q: What is the main complaint of the people who went to court?
options: The government ignored warnings and was not ready.

options: They are tired of accepting the situation.

articles.headline: Nobel Prize rewards the solution to life's mirror-image puzzle
articles.standfirst: Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai share the 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for explaining how nature – and chemists – can make just one 'hand' of a molecule.
body: Hold up your hands and look at them. They are mirror images of each other, yet no matter how you turn them, you cannot place one exactly on top of the other. Many of the molecules that make up living things share this curious property, which chemists call chirality. Amino acids, the building blocks of proteins, exist in both a 'left-handed' and a 'right-handed' form – but life on Earth uses almost exclusively one of them. Why nature should favour one hand so consistently has puzzled scientists for well over a century.

This year's Nobel Prize in Chemistry goes to two researchers who helped to solve that puzzle: the French chemist Henri B. Kagan, of Université Paris-Sud, and Kenso Soai, of the Tokyo University of Science. Together they will share the 12 million Swedish kronor that accompanies the award. 'This is one of the most exciting days of my life,' Professor Soai told the Nobel press conference by phone.

Their work unfolded over almost two decades. In 1986, Kagan found a way of steering chemical reactions so that they produced a far greater excess of one mirror form than anyone had believed possible. Soai took the idea further: in 1995 he described in the journal Nature a reaction that could, in principle, generate only the desired form, and by 2003 he had succeeded in controlling a reaction in which just one of the two mirror images appeared. In other words, they showed how 'homochirality' – a world of single-handed molecules – can emerge spontaneously.

The discovery is far from academic. In a laboratory, ordinary reactions tend to yield a 50–50 mixture of both forms, and in medicine the difference can be crucial: one version of a drug may cure a disease while its mirror image does nothing, or even causes harm. The tragedy of thalidomide in the 1950s and 1960s, when one form of the drug was effective but the other was toxic, remains the most painful reminder. Reactions that deliver only the right 'hand' therefore matter not only for our understanding of how life began, but for the safety of the medicines we take today.

glossary.d: the property of an object or molecule that is not identical to its mirror image, like a pair of hands
only; not including anything else
an amount that is more than another amount, or more than expected
to appear or develop naturally, without being caused from outside

questions.q: Why does the writer mention thalidomide?
options: to criticise the drug companies of the 1950s
to show that the prize could have been given earlier

articles.headline: An ID card for someone who doesn't exist
articles.standfirst: China has begun issuing official identification to AI-generated 'digital humans' – a step that supporters call protection and critics call surveillance.
body: Yuri was barely a year old when thousands of fans packed a concert hall on Shanghai's Bund to watch her perform. Projected on to a 100-metre screen, she sang in Mandarin and English and changed outfits in the blink of an eye. Yuri, however, is not a person. She is a virtual idol created by artificial intelligence – and, as of this year, she is also the first digital human in China to hold a government-backed identity card.

The card, issued under a pilot programme in Beijing, records her name, date of 'birth', address and facial features. Far from being a novelty, it has practical consequences: it allows her operators to open a digital-currency wallet in her name and to sign commercial deals in sectors ranging from fashion to gaming and cars. The same scheme has made her the country's first licensed AI artist.

The move reflects the sheer scale of the industry. A 2025 report from the Communication University of China counted at least 1.3 million firms linked to the digital-human sector, whose market was valued at around 48 billion yuan (US$10 billion) that year. Avatars that began as a way for streamers to remain anonymous have evolved into AI influencers capable of chatting with users in real time, and they now appear everywhere from news broadcasts and online shopping to short dramas. Last month, Beijing urged broadcasters and video platforms to register the digital humans they use.

Whether this is a sensible precaution or something more troubling depends on whom you ask. Supporters argue that registration protects intellectual property and makes it harder for criminals to use fake personas in online scams. Critics counter that giving the state a record of every virtual character extends surveillance into the metaverse. What is beyond dispute is that the line between a person and a product is becoming harder to draw – and that the rest of the world will soon have to decide where it stands.

glossary.d: a small-scale trial carried out before a plan is introduced more widely
something new and unusual that attracts interest, often only for a short time
used to emphasise how very large something is
the character or identity that someone presents to others
to reply to an argument by giving an opposing one
